name: Naproxen
summary: Naproxen is a painkiller that also treats inflammation, used for conditions such as period pain, back pain, gout and arthritis. It can cause ulcers and bleeding in the stomach or gut, so the lowest amount that works is used for the shortest time. Vomiting blood or passing black, tar-like poo needs a call to a GP or NHS 111 straight away.
usedFor: Joint and muscle pain and swelling, including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and gout
In the US, prescription naproxen is also used for juvenile arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis
howItWorks: Naproxen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). It works by reducing hormones that cause inflammation and pain in the body. This eases swelling and pain in joints and muscles.
onset: People usually start to feel better about 1 hour after taking naproxen. With regular use it can take up to about 3 days to work properly.

common: Constipation or diarrhoea, bloating and stomach pain, and feeling or being sick
Dizziness, feeling sleepy or tired, and headaches; headaches should usually go away after the first week
A rash and ringing in the ears
serious: Ulcer in the stomach or gut, more likely after long use or in big doses; vomiting blood or dark particles like coffee grounds, blood in the poo or black tar-like poo are signs of bleeding, and the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 now
Serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis): sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or very fast or difficult breathing, needs a 999 call
Chest pain, which could be a heart attack, needs a 999 call
Rarely, aseptic meningitis (fever, sickness, confusion, headache, neck stiffness, sensitivity to light), for which the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E
Confusion or blurred vision, after which the NHS advises waiting before driving

cautions: People who have had an allergic reaction to, or a serious side effect from, naproxen, ibuprofen, aspirin or another NSAID are advised not to take it
A past stomach ulcer or bleeding, or being at higher risk of an ulcer: a doctor may advise against naproxen or prescribe a stomach-protecting medicine alongside it
Kidney, liver or heart problems, high blood pressure, Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, lupus and blood-clotting disorders are on the NHS list for a doctor's check first
With kidney problems the NHS suggests talking to a doctor about the best anti-inflammatory to use
Asthma and allergies such as hay fever are listed by the NHS as reasons for a check before use
Not taken together with other NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or aspirin, because this raises the risk of serious side effects such as stomach ulcers

Interacting medicines named by the NHS include anticoagulants such as warfarin, steroids such as prednisolone and antidepressants such as citalopram, along with some diuretics, heart and blood pressure medicines and methotrexate
Alcohol can increase the risk of side effects such as stomach ulcers or bleeding, so the NHS advises limiting it
Not usually recommended in pregnancy and not usually used while breastfeeding; a doctor weighs benefit against risk
monitoring: MedlinePlus says the doctor may need to adjust other medicines or monitor more carefully for side effects. The NHS says a stomach-protecting medicine such as omeprazole or lansoprazole may be prescribed for people taking it long term or at risk of an ulcer.

sections.heading: What is naproxen used for?
sections.body:
Naproxen is a painkiller that also treats inflammation, and it belongs to the group of medicines called NSAIDs. The NHS says paracetamol is usually the best treatment for most types of pain, but naproxen is better for some types, such as period pain or back pain. It can also help with joint and muscle pain, gout, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, sprains and strains.

Naproxen comes as tablets or a liquid that is swallowed. Some types can be bought from pharmacies and others are available only on prescription. Adults and teenagers aged 15 and over can buy it from a pharmacy for period pain. MedlinePlus, a US source, says prescription naproxen treats osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. It says non-prescription naproxen is used for fever and mild pain such as headaches, muscle aches, menstrual pain, colds, toothaches and backaches.

sections.heading: How does naproxen work and how quickly?
sections.body:
Naproxen is an NSAID, and it works by reducing hormones that cause inflammation and pain in the body. The NHS says this reduces swelling and pain in joints and muscles. People usually start to feel better about 1 hour after taking it. With regular use it can take up to about 3 days to work properly.

The NHS advises that the lowest amount that controls symptoms is used for the shortest possible time. It also advises taking naproxen with or just after food to help protect the stomach.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of naproxen?
sections.body:
The NHS lists constipation or diarrhoea, dizziness, feeling sleepy or tired, bloating and stomach pain, headaches, feeling or being sick, a rash and ringing in the ears as common side effects. Headaches should usually go away after the first week. For dizziness, the NHS suggests sitting or lying down until the feeling passes.

Naproxen can cause an ulcer in the stomach or gut, especially after long use or in big doses. Vomiting blood or dark particles that look like coffee grounds, blood in the poo or black poo that looks like tar can be signs of bleeding in the stomach or gut. The NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 now if these happen.

A serious allergic reaction is rare, but sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or very fast or difficult breathing, needs a 999 call. Chest pain, which could be a heart attack, also needs a 999 call. The NHS also says to call 999 or go to A&E for possible aseptic meningitis, with fever, sickness, confusion, headache, neck stiffness and sensitivity to light.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with naproxen?
sections.body:
The NHS says naproxen is not suitable for people who have had an allergic reaction to, or a serious side effect from, naproxen, ibuprofen, aspirin or another NSAID. A doctor may advise against it for someone who has or has had a stomach ulcer, and may prescribe another medicine to protect the stomach when the risk is higher. The NHS also lists kidney, liver and heart problems, high blood pressure, Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, lupus, blood-clotting disorders, asthma and allergies such as hay fever as reasons to check with a doctor first.

With kidney problems, the NHS suggests talking to a doctor about the best anti-inflammatory to take. Some anti-inflammatories, including naproxen, are thought to slightly increase the chance of an irregular heartbeat, but the NHS says the chance is small and not enough to recommend people stop taking them. MedlinePlus says older adults are usually treated for short periods.

sections.heading: Naproxen with other medicines, alcohol and in pregnancy
sections.body:
The NHS says naproxen should not be taken at the same time as other NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or aspirin, because this raises the risk of serious side effects such as stomach ulcers. It can also interact with anticoagulants such as warfarin, steroid medicines such as prednisolone and antidepressants such as citalopram. A pharmacist or doctor can check a full medicines list.

The NHS says people can drink alcohol while taking naproxen, but limiting it is advised because alcohol can increase the risk of stomach ulcers or bleeding. In pregnancy, naproxen is not usually recommended because it may affect the baby, in particular their circulation and the level of amniotic fluid. Doctors will only advise it if the benefits clearly outweigh the risks. Naproxen passes into breast milk in small amounts and is unlikely to harm a baby, though there have been one or two reports of side effects in babies. Large amounts or long use of anti-inflammatories like naproxen can affect ovulation, which may make it harder to get pregnant.

faqs.q: Is naproxen the same as ibuprofen?
faqs.a: Both are NSAIDs, a group of painkillers that also reduce inflammation. The NHS advises against taking naproxen at the same time as another NSAID such as ibuprofen or aspirin. This is because it raises the risk of serious side effects such as stomach ulcers.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking naproxen?
faqs.a: The NHS says people can drink alcohol while taking naproxen. It advises limiting how much, because alcohol can increase the risk of side effects such as stomach ulcers or bleeding.

The NHS says naproxen will not usually affect the ability to drive, ride a bike or use machinery. If someone feels dizzy or tired or has problems with their vision after taking it, the NHS advises waiting until these effects have gone before driving.

faqs.q: Can I take naproxen in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says naproxen is not usually recommended in pregnancy because it may affect the baby, in particular their circulation and amniotic fluid levels. Doctors will only advise it if the benefits clearly outweigh the risks, and the NHS says paracetamol is usually the best painkiller in pregnancy.

faqs.q: Can I buy naproxen without a prescription?
faqs.a: In the UK some types of naproxen can be bought from a pharmacy and others are available only on prescription. Adults and teenagers aged 15 and over can buy it from a pharmacy for period pain.

faqs.q: When should I get urgent help with naproxen side effects?
faqs.a: Call 999 for sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, trouble breathing or chest pain. For vomiting blood, blood in the poo or black tar-like poo, the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 now.
